\chapter{Vivir --- the Family That Costs Nothing}
\label{ch:spanish-vivir}
\hlchaptermodality{34}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the singular of a regular -ir verb, and say why it asked me to learn no new form.}

In the singular the -ir endings ARE the -er endings; the families part company only in the plural.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vivir]{vivir — \textquotedblleft{}to live,\textquotedblright{} and the third family (that's barely new)}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-vivir}



\begin{quote}
The third and last verb family: \textbf{-ir}, and \textbf{vivir} (\textquotedblleft{}to live\textquotedblright{}) is your first. Here's the punchline — in the present tense, \textbf{-ir is almost identical to -er}. You've nearly finished learning the whole regular present.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{v-b} — Spanish \emph{v} = a soft \emph{b}: \emph{vivir} $\approx$ \emph{bee-BEER}.
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — one tap on the final \emph{r}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vivir} comes from Latin \textbf{vīvere}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to live\textquotedblright{}} — one of the most alive roots in English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{vivid} — \textquotedblleft{}full of life.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{survive} (\emph{super-vīvere}, \textquotedblleft{}to live beyond\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{revive} (\textquotedblleft{}live again\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{vivacious}, \textbf{convivial} (\textquotedblleft{}living together\textquotedblright{} — sociable), \textbf{viva!}, \textbf{vivarium}. (And \emph{vīta}, \textquotedblleft{}life,\textquotedblright{} gives \textbf{vital}, \textbf{vitamin}.)
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the family that costs nothing}]
The third family is the shortest lesson in this book, and it is short because of a fact rather than a shortcut.

\textbf{In the singular, the \emph{-ir} endings are the \emph{-er} endings.} Not similar. The same three:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{vivo} · \textbf{vives} · \textbf{vive} — \emph{-o}, \emph{-es}, \emph{-e}, exactly as \emph{como}, \emph{comes}, \emph{come}.
\end{quote}

So the third family asks you to learn no new form at all. You already built these three endings one at a time in the last chapter; here they are, doing the same work on a different verb.

The two families do part company later, in the plural — and when they do, you will meet that difference on its own. It is not needed now, and mentioning it here would be borrowing trouble.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vivir\textquotedblright{} — \emph{bee-BEER}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}como, comes, come\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}vivo, vives, vive\textquotedblright{} — identical endings
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vivir\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}vivid, survive, revive\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{vīvere} family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin verb is \emph{vivir} from, and two English cousins? (\emph{vīvere} — vivid, survive.) In the singular, how do \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} endings compare? (They are \textbf{identical}: \emph{-o / -es / -e}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I live.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Vivo}.) Next: a second verb in this family, and two words for asking questions.
\end{tcolorbox}
